children: The economic loss in the region around a pulp mill that closed in Alabama this spring could reach nearly $7 billion, according to a new study circulating around Southern statehouses and Washington, D.C.

The Coosa Pines, Ala., mill, which made absorbent material for diapers and sanitary products, was relatively small compared with the containerboard mills that have shuttered throughout the pine belt and left timber growers without buyers for much of their wood. Forester Tom Richardson and Larry Wall, a financial adviser to timberland owners, crunched the numbers to show Alabama's congressional delegation, business leaders and federal officials how economic losses extend beyond the more than 250 mill workers who lost jobs.
"It's a tidal wave that goes in all directions," Richardson said.

The bulk of the monetary loss is the mills' direct economic impact over 10 years, but they also tallied losses in a region encompassing about a million acres southeast of Birmingham from which the mill had sourced wood.

They included the collapse in pulpwood prices from about $7 a ton to zero in an 85-mile radius, which eliminates income and logging jobs and wrecks the net present value of timberland investments. They also considered the subsequent overcrowding of stands that would prevent trees from growing big enough to make lumber and utility poles and make swaths of timber susceptible to wood-boring beetles and total loss.
They added the impact to loggers making fewer, longer trips to more distant mills and plunging value of logging equipment such as feller-bunchers, delimbers and skidders.
If similar analysis is applied across the South everywhere pulpwood-consuming mills have closed, the losses exceed $100 billion and a case can be made for $200 billion, Richardson said.
